newsitem.title: USA: Jewell no longer suspect in Olympic bombing - judge.
newsitem.headline: Jewell no longer suspect in Olympic bombing - judge.

text.p: A federal judge, who says he believes Richard Jewell is no longer a suspect in the Olympic park bombing, has ordered authorities to release sealed documents showing why the former security guard fell under suspicion in the first place.

In a ruling issued late on Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Owen Forrester gave the Justice Department one week either to challenge his order in a federal appellate court or to unseal FBI affidavits used to obtain warrants to search Jewell's property.

Jewell, 33, who steadfastly maintains his innocence, has been the only named suspect in the bomb attack that left two dead and more than 100 wounded in downtown Atlanta on July 27. He has never been charged with a crime, despite months of searches, FBI surveillance and media scrutiny.

Now unemployed, Jewell is weighing the possibility of suing the federal government and several media outlets, saying news leaks about his role as a suspect and the resulting glare of publicity have ruined his chance of getting a job.

"The court concludes that the Jewell chapter of the Centennial Olympic Park bombing investigation has been closed. Most of its details have now become merely a historical footnote to the ongoing investigation," Forrester wrote in his ruling.
A spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office in Atlanta would say only that federal prosecutors were reviewing the order.
The judge has no authority over the bombing investigation and any move to clear Jewell formally would be up to the U.S. Attorney and the FBI.
U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno was asked during her weekly Justice Department news briefing in Washington if Jewell had been cleared as a suspect in the case.
"We have not made any decisions with respect to the investigation," she said. "The matter is pending. We should await further word."

In issuing his ruling, Forrester granted a motion by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and ABC-affiliate WSB-TV, which had asked the judge to unseal the documents. The same affidavits that were released to Jewell's legal team several weeks ago.

Jewell's criminal lawyer, Jack Martin, said Forrester's remarks are encouraging. "His instincts are very credible. He's speaking as an experienced judge and federal prosecutor, and saying that he doesn't see a whole lot going on in the case against Mr. Jewell," he told Reuters.

Martin, one of four attorneys Jewell has hired since finding himself at the center of the investigation, also said he believes the Justice Department may be only a week away from issuing a letter formally exonerating his client.

Earlier this month, Jewell's attorneys said he agreed to undergo a six-hour FBI interrogation with the understanding that federal authorities would clear his name publicly if satisified with his statements.
"We're probably a week or so away from getting a letter from the U.S. Attorney's Office. I've always thought we would get that," Martin said.

After the pipe bomb exploded in Centennial Olympic Park during a free outdoor concert, Jewell initially was hailed as a hero. He was working at a security guard at a nearby AT&T pavillion, when he alerted police to a suspicious green knapsack that contained the bomb and then helped clear crowds from the area before it detonated.
However, the news reports that soon named him as a suspect also said Jewell matched an FBI profile which described the likely suspect as a former police officer with an inclination towards heroism.
The Justice Department and FBI have begun a separate investigation to determine who leaked that information to the media.
